title: Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization
abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

The main approach for this is to generate multiple independent samples and select the best candidate via majority voting (Wang et al. , 2023 ) or verification against test cases (Jain et al. , 2024 ) . While such best-of- K K strategies reliably improve accuracy as K K increases, they scale inefficiently: each sample is generated without knowledge of prior attempts, leading to redundant exploration of similar trajectories. For problems that require long reasoning chains, where a single early error invalidates the entire generation, this redundancy is wasteful. Sequential multi-turn generation attempts to address this by incorporating environmental feedback into the context window (Madaan et al. , 2023 ) . The model generates a subsequent attempt conditioned on the failure of its previous output. However, sequential refinement often stagnates: when faced with genuinely difficult reasoning challenges, models frequently repeat similar logical errors across turns or fail to identify the precise point where the logic diverged (Kumar et al. , 2024 ) . The context window fills with unsuccessful attempts without yielding a correct solution. (A) Independent Sampling (BoN) Redundant compute (B) Sequential Refinement Feedback / Reprompt Feedback / Reprompt Evaluates only at end (C) TTEL Prefix Tree (Ours) × Error prune × Error Shared Prefix Localized error branching Figure 1: Search Tree Typology Comparison. (A) Independent Sampling generates entirely separate full-length trajectories, leading to high computational waste from parallel exploration of similar paths. (B) Sequential Refinement methods link full trajectories end-to-end, evaluating only at terminal steps. (C) TTEL structures search as a prefix-sharing tree, explicitly capitalizing on token-level error localization to branch exactly where reasoning diverges, avoiding redundant computation of shared prefixes and averting terminal failure. A deeper issue is that post-hoc feedback is inherently trajectory-conditional . When a candidate solution fails, the resulting feedback, such as an environment generated error, or self-generated critique, is informative about the specific reasoning path that produced that failure. If a model is restarted from scratch, it may never revisit the same intermediate states at which the feedback is most relevant. This creates a fundamental mismatch: the supervision is path-specific, but existing inference-time strategies such as sequential refinement largely apply it as though it were a global revision signal. Tree-structured search methods, such as Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. , 2023 ) , offer an alternative by exploring multiple reasoning paths and backtracking. These methods typically operate at the level of coarse reasoning steps, relying on self-evaluation heuristics to prune branches. Population-based approaches like Recursive Self-Aggregation (Venkatraman et al. , 2025 ) refine solutions by aggregating information across a pool of candidates. Both families of methods improve over flat sampling, but neither leverages fine-grained, token-level signals about where reasoning went wrong. Essentially, these existing approaches either lose the state on which feedback is informative, or preserve the state without extracting a precise corrective signal from it. This suggests a more targeted view of inference-time improvement: rather than treating feedback as a generic instruction for a fresh retry, can a model use feedback to localize error on the specific trajectory that produced it , retain the useful prefix of that trajectory, and selectively regenerate only the suffix where the reasoning becomes suspect? Motivated by this question, we investigate the following core problem: Can an LLM perform token-level credit assignment on its own failed trajectories, and leverage this localized signal to guide test-time scaling optimally? We propose TTEL , an inference-time search algorithm that performs token-level error localization without gradient updates. When a generated solution fails, we prompt the model with the environmental feedback to re-evaluate the original trajectory via prompt log-probabilities. By comparing token probabilities before and after observing this feedback, we identify positions of maximal disagreement. A sharp drop in probability indicates that the model strongly rejects its prior decision at that specific step. To ensure these probability shifts are genuinely driven by the feedback rather than generic context changes, we filter the signal against a baseline with non-diagnostic feedback. TTEL then uses this localized signal to truncate the reasoning trace at the highest-confidence error and branch a new generation from that point. By directing computation toward correcting specific mistakes rather than regenerating entire solutions, this feedback-guided tree search achieves substantially higher token efficiency than standard sampling baselines across diverse reasoning tasks, including competitive programming (Jain et al. , 2024 ) and complex mathematical reasoning (Balunovic et al. , 2025 ) . Our Contributions. Primarily, this paper shows that LLMs can error correct failing trajectories at inference time based on feedback, and use it to guide test-time search. Specifically: 1. Token-Level Error Localization: We introduce TTEL , an inference-time algorithm that uses probability contrasts by comparing informed environmental feedback against non-diagnostic feedback to localize errors during generation. 2. Efficient Test-Time Search: By coupling local credit assignment with trajectory retention, TTEL truncates and branches only the faulty suffix of a trajectory. This maximizes the reuse of valid reasoning prefixes and eliminates the redundant exploration. 3. Empirical Efficiency: We establish strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across math benchmarks like AIME-2025, and coding benchmarks like LiveCodeBench where TTEL attains pass@64 of 71.0% at roughly half the token cost of independent sampling. 2 Related Work We provide an abbreviated overview of related work below; an extended discussion mapping TTEL to the broader literature is available in Appendix A . Test-Time Scaling and Tree Search. Reasoning performance scales reliably with inference-time compute (Snell et al. , 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) , typically through robust independent sampling arrays (Wang et al. , 2023 ) . To iterate beyond flat sampling, sequential refinement methods prepend execution feedback to prompt self-correction (Madaan et al. , 2023 ; Klissarov et al. , 2026 ) . However, because they treat trajectory-specific feedback as a global instruction, these models often regenerate reasoning from scratch, triggering context bloat or hallucinated logic (Kumar et al. , 2024 ) . Structured backtracking algorithms like Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. , 2023 ) and population-based search (Venkatraman et al. , 2025 ) remedy this by exploring partial branches, but they rely on programmatic chunking and external heuristics rather than internal, token-level signals. On-Policy Distillation and Preference Optimization. Recent work has increasingly utilized natural language assessment for dense credit assignment. By evaluating the ratio between a base policy and a feedback-conditioned teacher, methods like Generalized Knowledge Distillation (Agarwal et al. , 2024 ) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (Zhao et al. , 2026 ) optimize student models directly on their own generated rollouts. This core mathematical insight, minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence driven by π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) / π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , f ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)/\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,f) , has established the foundation for new reinforcement learning algorithms, most notably Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO; Hübotter et al. 2026 ) and RLTF (Song et al. , 2026 ) . Similar mechanisms have also been applied successfully in experiential context distillation (OPCD; Ye et al. 2026 ) and continual learning (SDFT; Shenfeld et al. 2026 ). Repurposing the Signal for Inference-Time Search. Crucially, this existing body of work restricts the application of the π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) / π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , f ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)/\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,f) divergence to offline gradient updates, yielding static policy networks. The direct capability of this ratio to localize errors purely as an online, inference-time heuristic has remained fundamentally unaddressed. TTEL bridges this gap by repurposing the token-level signal used in the SDPO framework. Specifically, TTEL extracts an organic, native pruning criterion that structures and bounds test-time search without requiring parameter updates. 3 Preliminaries and Problem Formulation Let π θ \pi_{\theta} denote a pre-trained autoregressive language model over vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Given a problem prompt x x , the model generates a trajectory y = ( y 1 , … , y N ) y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{N}) with token probabilities p t ( S ) := π θ ​ ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) , y < t := ( y 1 , … , y t − 1 ) . p_{t}^{(S)}:=\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}),\qquad y_{<t}:=(y_{1},\dots,y_{t-1}). (1) For a realized trajectory y y , we refer to p t ( S ) p_{t}^{(S)} as the student token probability , i.e., the probability assigned to the generated token y t y_{t} during the original rollout. We assume access to an execution environment ℰ \mathcal{E} , which evaluates a candidate trajectory y y on problem x x and returns a textual feedback string f f . The central challenge in test-time scaling is a credit assignment bottleneck : when a generated trajectory fails, the environment evaluates the trajectory globally, but does not identify the specific token position at which the reasoning first became inconsistent with a successful solution. Standard best-of- K K sampling discards failed trajectories entirely, while sequential refinement conditions on feedback but does not explicitly localize where to revise the trajectory. Our goal is to use the model itself to perform token-level post-hoc error localization on a failed trajectory, and then use that localized signal to guide branching during inference-time search. 4 Methodology TTEL operates on a single pre-trained language model π θ \pi_{\theta} that serves as both the generator and the evaluator of its own outputs. The core mechanism computes the same token-level divergence signal that train-time self-distillation algorithms use to update model weights (Hübotter et al. , 2026 ) , but instead of aggregating this signal into a gradient step, TTEL uses it to prune and branch an inference-time search tree. In this case, the algorithm performs a restart from the original prompt x x . 5 The TTEL Algorithm Algorithm 1 summarizes the full TTEL procedure. The search tree 𝒯 \mathcal{T} stores retained prefixes of previously generated trajectories, with the root corresponding to the empty prefix. At each iteration, the algorithm selects a leaf prefix y < t y_{<t} from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and generates a full candidate continuation conditioned on both the original problem prompt x x and the retained prefix. The resulting trajectory is then evaluated by the execution environment ℰ \mathcal{E} , which returns feedback f f for re-scoring and subsequent regeneration. The diagnostic component of f f may contain environment-derived information, such as a compiler error, runtime error, or failing public test case. The algorithm performs token-level spike detection by re-scoring the same trajectory under two alternative contexts: a feedback-conditioned context using the actual feedback f f , and a null-feedback context using a non-diagnostic message f ∅ f_{\varnothing} . This yields a feedback-conditioned spike score Δ t ​ ( f ) = p t ( S ) − p t ( T ) ​ ( f ) \Delta_{t}(f)=p_{t}^{(S)}-p_{t}^{(T)}(f) and a baseline spike score Δ t ​ ( f ∅ ) = p t ( S ) − p t ( B ) ​ ( f ∅ ) \Delta_{t}(f_{\varnothing})=p_{t}^{(S)}-p_{t}^{(B)}(f_{\varnothing}) at each token position. The filtered spike score g t = Δ t ​ ( f ) − Δ t ​ ( f ∅ ) g_{t}=\Delta_{t}(f)-\Delta_{t}(f_{\varnothing}) captures disagreement that is specific to the observed failure signal rather than generic context augmentation. The algorithm then constructs the localized error set E = { t ∣ Δ t ​ ( f ) > τ ∧ Δ t ​ ( f ∅ ) ≤ τ B } , E=\{\,t\mid\Delta_{t}(f)>\tau\;\land\;\Delta_{t}(f_{\varnothing})\leq\tau_{B}\,\}, which contains token positions whose probability drops sharply under true feedback but not under null feedback. If this set is nonempty, TTEL selects the branch point t ∗ = arg ⁡ max t ∈ E ⁡ g t t^{*}=\arg\max_{t\in E}g_{t} and adds the retained prefix y < t ∗ y_{<t^{*}} to the tree. A subsequent generation from this prefix reuses the earlier portion of the trajectory while revising the region where the model exhibits the strongest feedback-specific disagreement. If no actionable spike is detected, the algorithm performs a restart by adding the empty prefix back into the tree, thereby encouraging continued exploration from scratch rather than overcommitting to an uninformative failed trajectory. The procedure repeats until the inference-time budget K K is exhausted, where the budget may be measured in generated tokens, completed trajectories, or environment calls. The procedure returns the generated candidate set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , which is evaluated using pass@ k k . An external selector, such as a verifier score, execution outcome, or majority-based aggregation, may optionally be applied when a single answer is required. In this way, TTEL converts token-level self-re-evaluation into an explicit tree-search policy that adaptively allocates computation toward revising localized errors instead of repeatedly regenerating entire solutions. 6 Theoretical Analysis Notation. Let x x be the problem, y y a failed trajectory, and f f the corresponding feedback, which includes y y . Let c = ( x , f ) c=(x,f) denote this shared context. Suppose TTEL selects a branch point t ∗ t^{*} and retains the anchor prefix a = y < t ∗ a=y_{<t^{*}} . We compare two post-failure strategies: 1. Restart: Generating a fresh attempt from the context without anchoring, Y R ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ c ) Y^{\mathrm{R}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c) . 2. Branch: Forcing generation to begin from the anchor prefix, Y B ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ c , a ) Y^{\mathrm{B}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c,a) . Let V ​ ( y ^ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } V(\hat{y})\in\{0,1\} denote whether candidate y ^ \hat{y} correctly solves the problem. Theorem 1 (Branching Advantage) . Assume autoregressive prefix consistency , meaning that freely generating a sequence that begins with a a is distributionally equivalent to explicitly anchoring generation at a a : ℒ ​ ( Y ≥ | a | + 1 R | Y < | a | + 1 R = a , c ) = ℒ ​ ( Y ≥ | a | + 1 B | c , a ) . \mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{\mathrm{R}}_{\geq|a|+1}\bigm|Y^{\mathrm{R}}_{<|a|+1}=a,\,c\bigr)=\mathcal{L}\bigl(Y^{\mathrm{B}}_{\geq|a|+1}\bigm|c,a\bigr). Let p a = Pr ⁡ ( Y R ​ begins with ​ a ∣ c ) p_{a}=\Pr(Y^{\mathrm{R}}\text{ begins with }a\mid c) be the probability that a restart naturally recovers the anchor prefix. Let s a s_{a} and s ¬ a s_{\neg a} be the probability of success given that the generation does, or does not, begin with a a . Then: Pr ⁡ ( V ​ ( Y B ) = 1 ∣ c , a ) − Pr ⁡ ( V ​ ( Y R ) = 1 ∣ c ) = ( 1 − p a ) ​ ( s a − s ¬ a ) . \Pr\bigl(V(Y^{\mathrm{B}})\!=\!1\mid c,a\bigr)-\Pr\bigl(V(Y^{\mathrm{R}})\!=\!1\mid c\bigr)\;=\;(1-p_{a})(s_{a}-s_{\neg a}). Proof. By prefix consistency, the success rate of branching is exactly the success rate of restart conditioned on recovering the prefix: Pr ⁡ ( V ​ ( Y B ) = 1 ) = s a \Pr(V(Y^{\mathrm{B}})\!=\!1)=s_{a} . By the law of total probability, the unconditional success rate of restart is: Pr ⁡ ( V ​ ( Y R ) = 1 ) = p a ​ s a + ( 1 − p a ) ​ s ¬ a . \Pr(V(Y^{\mathrm{R}})\!=\!1)=p_{a}s_{a}+(1-p_{a})s_{\neg a}. Subtracting the second equation from the first yields the result. ∎ The theorem formally justifies the TTEL branching mechanism over standard sequential refinement. Verifier feedback f f is trajectory-conditional: it provides correction specifically relevant to the reasoning state at the anchor prefix a a . A restart strategy generated from scratch ( Y R Y^{\mathrm{R}} ) may never naturally return to this necessary intermediate state ( p a ≪ 1 p_{a}\ll 1 ), rendering the feedback useless or misleading. Takeaway Branching structurally guarantees that the generation is anchored exactly where the feedback’s correction becomes actionable. It strictly improves over sequential restart as long as success is more likely once the correct prefix is reached ( s a > s ¬ a s_{a}>s_{\neg a} ). 7 Experiments In this section, we outline our experimental framework designed to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, TTEL . We focus our evaluation on two challenging domains demanding multi-step planning: complex mathematical reasoning and code generation. Our empirical evaluation is designed to answer the following core research questions (RQ): • RQ1 (Compute Scalability & Generalization): How efficiently does TTEL scale inference-time compute to uncover correct trajectories compared to standard multi-turn paradigms, and does this scaling advantage generalize across environments with and without explicit verification feedback? • RQ2 (The Role of Context in Error Localization): How strictly does accurate token-level credit assignment depend on the availability of rich environment execution signals and the retention of the historical reasoning trace? • RQ3 (Filtering Noise vs. Semantic Signal): Is the null-feedback baseline subtraction strictly necessary to isolate genuine, feedback-driven model corrections from generic context-induced probability shifts? Evaluation Benchmarks To rigorously assess the capabilities of our approach, we focus on the following two benchmark categories: • Mathematical Reasoning: We evaluate on AIME-25 dataset, and HMMT-25 from the MathArena benchmark (Balunovic et al. , 2025 ) . Each dataset consists of 30 highly challenging, competition-level mathematics problems designed to test deep, multi-step analytical reasoning without intermediate execution feedback. • Code Generation: We utilize LiveCodeBench (Jain et al. , 2024 ) , specifically a recent subset of 131 contest-style coding questions released between February and May 2025. This benchmark optionally provides rigorous execution feedback via public test cases. We define two variants for our method based on the feedback: • TTEL -GenFB: This uses generic feedback which includes previous answers, the full reasoning trace for the last attempt, a static error message (“Your previous attempt was unsuccessful.”) and a re-attempt instruction. This is applicable for all benchmarks. • TTEL -EnvFB: The static error message in TTEL -GenFB is replaced by rich environment feedback such as runtime errors or failing public test cases. This can be tested on LiveCodeBench as it provides execution based feedback, but not on maths benchmarks. Implementation Details We utilize the Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 models for our experiments. To compare inference-time scaling across methods, we report both the rollout budget k k and the total number of generated tokens . The maximum generation limit per attempt is capped at 16,384 tokens. Decoding across all methods uses a temperature T = 1 T=1 and top p = 1 \text{top}_{p}=1 . For TTEL , we use a localized spike detection threshold of τ = 0.06 \tau=0.06 and maintain a maximum checkpoint depth of D c = 16 , 384 D_{c}=16,384 . To standardize evaluation, our primary metric is pass@ k k , measuring whether at least one of the k k adaptively generated rollouts produces a correct solution. Baselines To isolate the performance gains of TTEL , we compare our method against three robust test-time scaling baselines: 1. Independent Sampling: A standard parallel generation (best-of- k k ) approach. The model independently generates k k full rollouts, and we evaluate whether any trajectory successfully solves the problem. 2. Multi-turn Refinement: A sequential feedback-driven approach. The model is allowed a maximum of k k interactive turns to arrive at the correct answer, where each subsequent attempt is conditioned on the full sequence of previous attempts and their respective execution feedback. 3. Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA): A recent population-based test-time scaling algorithm that searches through a parameter space characterized by population size N N , aggregation size K K , and a distinct number of sequential steps T T . 8 Experimental Results We structure our results to directly address the research questions outlined in Section 7 . We evaluate both TTEL -GenFB and TTEL -EnvFB to measure the impact of informative environment feedback. To demonstrate the necessity of Full Thought Trace from the previous attempt, we include ablations that utilize only final answers from previous attempts. Accurate token-level credit assignment depends on the context provided to the teacher during spike detection. We hypothesize that retention of the original thought trace y y , and the specificity of the external feedback f f can enable more precise error-localization. As illustrated in Figure 7 , blinding the teacher to the Full Trace generated by the student and conditioning execution failure solely on the extracted final answer causes a severe drop in pass@ k k (from 0.630 to 0.597 in case of TTEL-GenFB ) alongside inflated token consumption. Accurate mistake localization algebraically requires the model to review the logic that actually produced the error, rendering the Full Trace strictly necessary. Furthermore, advancing beyond generic feedback by injecting explicit execution traces aggressively grounds the probability distribution. This explicit external signal triggers far more precise log-probability divergences than implicit self-correction, lowering search cost and boosting pass@ k k to 0.658 for TTEL-EnvFB . Ultimately, token-efficient search relies on maximizing diagnostic context f f during re-scoring. 8.3 Isolating Semantic Signals via Baseline Filtering (RQ3) Finally, we validate the core architectural component of TTEL : the unconditional (null) baseline filter, Δ t ​ ( f ∅ ) \Delta_{t}(f_{\varnothing}) . While differences in student and teacher probabilities can identify divergence in reasoning due to genuine mistakes, the updated context for the teacher also induces a baseline probability shift. For example, the teacher may try to rephrase or abridge the reasoning trace of the student, leading to a large number of false-positive spikes that are unsuitable for diverging into novel branches. This ablation utilizes raw teacher probability spikes Δ t ​ ( f ) \Delta_{t}(f) to trigger branching, entirely removing the secondary null-feedback baseline subtraction. As shown in Figure 8 , removing this filter dramatically changes the search dynamics. The average number of detected spikes in Turn 1 explodes from 19.3 to 486.0, representing massive false-positive mistake detections driven merely by context augmentation rather than genuine error correction. This noisy search degrades downstream pass@ k k to 0.592. Thus, the baseline filter is strictly required to normalize the signal, filter context-induced probability shifts, and accurately localize actionable mathematical or logical errors. Conclusion: In this work, we introduced Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization ( TTEL ), demonstrating that LLMs can perform precise token-level credit assignment at inference time without gradient updates. By coupling localized error detection directly with trajectory retention, TTEL maximally reuses valid reasoning prefixes and mitigates computational redundancy. Our results establish new compute-optimal Pareto frontiers, across math and coding tasks. References R. Agarwal, N. Vieillard, Y. Zhou, P. Stanczyk, S. R. Garea, M. Geist, and O.
